extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in epic poetry and poetic practice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance on composing and judging epic poetry (with examples drawn from Milton), plus a few prescriptive notes on poetly character, boarding-school curriculum, and audience etiquette appearing in the same issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a subject conformable to your genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace advises a Poet to consider thoroughly the Nature and Force of his Genius; a poet should choose a Subject entirely conformable to those Talents of which he is master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Milton 'seems to have known perfectly well, wherein his Strength lay, and has therefore chosen a Subject entirely conformable to those Talents' — his genius being disposed to the sublime, he chose the noblest subject (Chaos, Creation, Heaven, Earth and Hell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a noble, vast subject when your genius suits the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet's genius inclines to the sublime, the subject ought to be the noblest that can enter into the thoughts of man — everything that is truly great and astonishing should have a place in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's epic includes the whole system of the intellectual world; use large-scale material (creation, fall, heaven/hell) to suit a sublimity-directed imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict Divine Persons with reverence and theological sobriety
rubrics_metrics.description: When Divine Persons are introduced as speakers the poet should proceed with a kind of fear and trembling, confining himself to thoughts and expressions drawn from orthodox divines and Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such speeches should aim to raise 'Divine Love and Religious Fear' rather than display poetical pomp; the beauties to be sought are devotional rather than purely poetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat abstruse doctrinal matter with shortness and perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular beauty of speeches treating complicated Christian doctrines consists in shortness and perspicuity of style, which can couch great mysteries clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's Third Book is praised for representing predestination, free-will, incarnation, redemption with clarity and concentrated expression; intersperse appropriate poetic graces but keep the doctrinal exposition concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance the probable and the marvellous in the epic fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's rule: the fable of an epic poem should abound in circumstances both credible and astonishing — the probable and the marvellous should be reconciled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a fable is only probable it is mere history; if only marvellous it is romance. The 'great secret' of heroic poetry is to produce both belief and astonishment in the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use supernatural machinery to render wonders credible
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles and surprising incidents become acceptable when the poet invents agents of a superior nature (gods, angels) capable of effecting the wonderful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transformations in Homer and Virgil (gods turning ships into rocks, fleets into nymphs) — such machinery makes the marvellous plausible within the poem's world; Milton's angels serve a similar purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid astonishing passages that lack credibility (avoid dream-like episodes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages that are astonishing yet not credible (descriptions of dreams, shadows, the Limbo of Vanity, certain episodes of Sin and Death) weaken the poem because the reader cannot accept them as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: some of Milton's 'shadowy' passages are 'the Description of Dreams and Shadows, not of Things or Persons' — such excrescences should be judged or pruned as they reduce poetic probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the plain literal sense appear probable to ordinary readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides allegorical or hidden meanings, the plain literal sense of the story ought to appear probable; the story should be such as an ordinary reader may acquiesce in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle and the ancients sometimes used real names to lend credibility; the poem should contain natural, moral, or political truths that sensible readers can recognize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recognized historical or famous names to increase credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient tragic writers used the names of great men to make subjects more credible; invoking familiar personages helps a reader accept extraordinary actions as plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device was used intentionally by tragedians to provide probability for events that did not literally occur to the historical figures invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ an omniscient, large-scale survey to achieve grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: A survey of the whole Creation and every thing transacted in it is a prospect worthy of omniscience and produces a sublime effect far above smaller or more local description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's panoramic descriptions (God's view of creation, Satan's walk on the outside of the universe, the silence of the angels, hymns of angels) are cited as models of noble, grand imaginative perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be attentive to excesses and excrescences in majestic poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all elevated or celebrated passages are essential; some (e.g., the celebrated Complaint that opens Milton's Third Book) may be an excrescence rather than a necessary part of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consider whether glorious digressions truly serve the poem's unity and probability, and cut or restrain those that feel superfluous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/breeding qualification for a good poet or playwright
rubrics_metrics.description: In a question about the chief qualification of a good Poet, the Spectator replies: 'To be a very well-bred Man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as pithy advice: poetic skill is paired with social refinement and manners (this is asserted as the primary 'qualification' in the correspondence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boarding-school curriculum for young gentlewomen (prescriptive advertisement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The advertised Boarding-School will teach, besides common accomplishments, 'the whole Art of Paistrey and Preserving, with whatever may render them accomplished.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also implied (by contemporary expectations): needlework, dancing, and the French tongue are part of the usual accomplishments; the advertisement functions as a prescriptive list of what such schools should teach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lazy, overused compliments in lovers' letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Lovers writing to the Spectator are desired to forbear the common expression 'She has in her all that is valuable in Woman' as lazy and untrue for most cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stylistic injunction discouraging stock phrases and urging more inventive, truthful compliments in epistolary or amorous address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience etiquette claim: visual actions may merit repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A correspondent argues that when an audience cries 'Altro Volto' (encore) it should be as acceptable to demand a graceful action be repeated as to ask for a pleasing sound to be sung again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an asserted norm for equitable treatment of visual and auditory pleasures in stage performances — the correspondent expects reasoned justification from performers when refusing such requests.
